questions.assertion: In the gold foil experiment, most of the alpha particles passed through the thin gold foil without any deflection.
questions.reason: Most of the space inside an atom is empty.
questions.answer: a
questions.explanation: Both are true, and R explains A: because most of an atom is empty space, most alpha particles met nothing in their path and went straight through. This was one of Rutherford's main conclusions.

questions.assertion: The isotopes of an element have similar chemical properties.
questions.reason: The isotopes of an element have the same number of neutrons in their nuclei.
questions.answer: c
questions.explanation: A is true: isotopes have the same number of electrons and the same electronic configuration, so their chemical properties are similar. R is false: isotopes differ in the number of neutrons, which is why their mass numbers differ.

questions.stem: Arrange the atomic models of Bohr, Dalton, Rutherford and Thomson in the order in which they were proposed. Write one new idea introduced by Thomson's model and one by Rutherford's model.
questions.answer: Order: Dalton → Thomson → Rutherford → Bohr. Thomson: the atom is a sphere of positive charge with electrons distributed throughout it (the plum pudding model). Rutherford: the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus at the centre, with electrons revolving around it.
valuePoints: Correct order: Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford, Bohr
Thomson: electrons spread in a sphere of positive charge
Rutherford: small dense positively charged nucleus with electrons revolving around it

rubric.label: Order of models
rubric.descriptor: Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford, Bohr in that order; no mark if any two are interchanged

rubric.label: New ideas
rubric.descriptor: ½ mark for Thomson's positive sphere with embedded electrons; ½ mark for Rutherford's nucleus

questions.stem: An atom has 17 protons in its nucleus and a mass number of 37. Find the number of (i) neutrons and (ii) electrons in this atom.
questions.answer: (i) Number of neutrons = mass number − number of protons = 37 − 17 = 20. (ii) The atom is electrically neutral, so the number of electrons equals the number of protons = 17.
valuePoints: Uses mass number = protons + neutrons to get 20 neutrons
Electrons = protons = 17 because the atom is neutral

rubric.label: Electrons
rubric.descriptor: 17, with the reason that a neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons

questions.stem: Calcium (atomic number 20), potassium (atomic number 19) and argon (atomic number 18) each have atoms with a mass number of 40. What name is given to such atoms? Find the number of neutrons in each of these atoms.
questions.answer: Atoms of different elements with the same mass number but different atomic numbers are called isobars. Neutrons = mass number − atomic number: calcium 40 − 20 = 20; potassium 40 − 19 = 21; argon 40 − 18 = 22.
valuePoints: Names them isobars
Neutrons: calcium 20, potassium 21, argon 22

rubric.label: Term
rubric.descriptor: Isobars, with the idea of same mass number but different atomic numbers

rubric.label: Neutron counts
rubric.descriptor: All three correct; ½ mark for two correct

questions.stem: Rutherford's model could not explain why atoms are stable. Explain this limitation, and state how Bohr's model overcame it.
questions.answer: In Rutherford's model electrons revolve around the nucleus in circular paths. A particle moving in a circle keeps changing direction, so it is accelerating, and an accelerating charged electron should lose energy. Losing energy, it would spiral inwards and fall into the positively charged nucleus, and the atom would collapse — but atoms are actually stable. Bohr proposed that electrons revolve only in certain fixed shells (stationary states or energy levels), and that while moving in such a shell an electron has a definite energy and does not lose energy, so it does not fall into the nucleus.
valuePoints: Revolving electron is accelerating and should lose energy
It would spiral into the nucleus and the atom would collapse
Bohr: electrons in fixed shells (stationary states) do not lose energy

rubric.label: Accelerating electron loses energy
rubric.descriptor: Circular motion means acceleration; an accelerating electron should lose energy

rubric.label: Collapse of atom
rubric.descriptor: Electron spirals into the nucleus, so atoms would not be stable

rubric.label: Bohr's stationary states
rubric.descriptor: Electrons move only in fixed shells of definite energy and do not lose energy there

questions.stem: The nucleus of an atom of element X contains 14 neutrons, and its mass number is 27. (i) Find its atomic number and identify the element. (ii) Write its electronic configuration. (iii) What is its valency? Give a reason.
questions.answer: (i) Atomic number = mass number − neutrons = 27 − 14 = 13. The element with atomic number 13 is aluminium (Al). (ii) 13 electrons are filled K, L, M: 2, 8, 3. (iii) It has 3 valence electrons, fewer than four, so it tends to lose these 3 electrons to attain an octet; its valency is 3.
valuePoints: Atomic number 13, aluminium
Electronic configuration 2, 8, 3
Valency 3 because it loses its 3 valence electrons

rubric.label: Atomic number and element
rubric.descriptor: Z = 13 (½) and aluminium (½)

rubric.label: Valency with reason
rubric.descriptor: 3 (½); loses three valence electrons to complete the octet (½)

questions.stem: An element Y occurs in nature as two isotopes of masses 63 u and 65 u, present in the ratio 70% : 30%. Calculate the weighted average atomic mass of Y. Why is this value different from the simple average of the two masses?
questions.answer: Weighted average atomic mass = (63 × 70/100) + (65 × 30/100) = 44.1 + 19.5 = 63.6 u. The simple average would be (63 + 65)/2 = 64 u. The simple average treats both isotopes as equally common, but the lighter isotope makes up 70% of the atoms, so the weighted average, which takes the relative abundance into account, lies closer to 63 u.
valuePoints: Multiplies each mass by its percentage abundance and adds
Weighted average = 63.6 u
Simple average 64 u ignores that the isotopes are not equally abundant

rubric.label: Weighted average
rubric.descriptor: 63.6 u, with unit

rubric.label: Why it differs
rubric.descriptor: Simple average (64 u) ignores relative abundance; the more common isotope pulls the average towards 63 u

questions.stem: Describe Thomson's model of the atom. Explain how the gold foil experiment tested this model: what result was expected, what was actually observed, and what conclusions Rutherford drew about the structure of the atom.
questions.answer: Thomson's model: the atom is a sphere of positive charge with negatively charged electrons distributed throughout it, so that the charges balance (plum pudding or watermelon model). Gold foil experiment: Geiger and Marsden, working under Rutherford, aimed a narrow beam of positively charged alpha particles at an extremely thin gold foil. Expected: since the positive charge was thought to be spread out evenly, the alpha particles should pass straight through or be deflected only slightly. Observed: most alpha particles passed through undeflected, some were deflected through large angles, and a few even bounced back. Conclusions: (i) most of an atom is empty space, since most particles passed through; (ii) the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a tiny, dense region at the centre called the nucleus, which caused the large deflections and rebounds; (iii) the nucleus is extremely small compared with the atom (about 10⁵ times smaller), and the electrons revolve around it like planets around the Sun.
valuePoints: Thomson: sphere of positive charge with electrons spread through it
Alpha particles aimed at a thin gold foil
Expected: pass straight or deflect slightly
Observed: most undeflected, some deflected at large angles, a few bounced back
Conclusions: mostly empty space; small dense positive nucleus with most of the mass; electrons revolve around it

rubric.label: Thomson's model
rubric.descriptor: Positive sphere with electrons distributed throughout

rubric.label: Set-up and expectation
rubric.descriptor: Alpha particles on thin gold foil (½); expected little or no deflection because charge spread evenly (½)

rubric.label: Observations
rubric.descriptor: Most undeflected, some large-angle deflections, a few bounced back; ½ mark for two of three

rubric.label: Empty space
rubric.descriptor: Most of the atom is empty space, linked to undeflected particles

rubric.label: Nucleus
rubric.descriptor: Tiny dense nucleus holding all positive charge and most mass (½); electrons revolve around it (½)

questions.stem: State the rules suggested by Bohr and Bury for filling electrons in shells. Using them, write the electronic configurations of the elements with atomic numbers 8, 11, 16 and 18, give the number of valence electrons and the valency of each, and name the element that is largely unreactive.
questions.answer: Rules: (1) the maximum number of electrons in a shell is 2n², so K holds 2, L holds 8 and M holds 18; (2) the outermost shell can hold at most 8 electrons; (3) shells are filled stepwise from the one nearest the nucleus, in the order K, L, M, N. Configurations: Z = 8 (oxygen) 2, 6 — 6 valence electrons, gains 2, valency 2. Z = 11 (sodium) 2, 8, 1 — 1 valence electron, loses 1, valency 1. Z = 16 (sulfur) 2, 8, 6 — 6 valence electrons, gains 2, valency 2. Z = 18 (argon) 2, 8, 8 — 8 valence electrons, a complete octet, so it neither gains nor loses electrons (valency 0). Argon is largely unreactive because its octet is already complete.
valuePoints: 2n² rule, at most 8 in the outermost shell, stepwise filling K, L, M
Configurations 2,6; 2,8,1; 2,8,6; 2,8,8
Valence electrons 6, 1, 6, 8
Valencies 2, 1, 2 and 0
Argon unreactive: complete octet

rubric.label: Bohr–Bury rules
rubric.descriptor: ½ mark each for 2n², maximum 8 in outermost shell, stepwise filling

rubric.label: Configurations
rubric.descriptor: All four correct; 1 mark for three, ½ for two

rubric.label: Valence electrons and valency
rubric.descriptor: All four valencies with valence electrons; ½ mark deducted per error

rubric.label: Unreactive element
rubric.descriptor: Argon, because of its complete octet

questions.passage: At a school science exhibition, Meera prepared a chart on the three isotopes of carbon, written as carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14. Each has 6 protons and 6 electrons, and carbon-12 is the most abundant in nature. Beside it she listed some uses of isotopes: an isotope of uranium is used as fuel in nuclear reactors to generate electricity, a radioactive isotope of cobalt is used in radiation treatment for cancer, an isotope of iodine is used to treat goitre, and one of the carbon isotopes is used by archaeologists and geologists to find the age of ancient fossils and artefacts. A visitor asked her why the three carbon isotopes behave alike in chemical reactions even though their masses are different.

parts.prompt: Which isotope of carbon is used to determine the age of ancient fossils and artefacts?
parts.answer: (c) Carbon-14 is the isotope used in archaeology and geology to find the age of fossils and artefacts.

parts.prompt: How many neutrons are present in an atom of carbon-14?
Answer the visitor's question: why do the isotopes of carbon have similar chemical properties but different masses?
parts.answer: They have the same number of electrons (6) and the same electronic configuration (2, 4), and chemical properties depend mainly on valence electrons, so they react alike (1 mark). They differ in the number of neutrons (6, 7 and 8), so their mass numbers and masses differ (1 mark).

questions.assertion: The molecular mass of carbon dioxide (CO₂) is 44 u, taking the atomic masses C = 12 u and O = 16 u.
questions.reason: Carbon dioxide is a covalent compound in which the atoms are held together by shared pairs of electrons.
questions.answer: b
questions.explanation: Both are true, but R does not explain A. The molecular mass comes from adding the atomic masses: 12 + (16 × 2) = 44 u. The type of bond in the molecule is a separate fact.

questions.assertion: When 10 g of ethanol is burnt in an open beaker and no residue is left, this shows that mass is not conserved in the reaction.
questions.reason: In a chemical reaction, the total mass of the products is equal to the total mass of the reactants.
questions.answer: d
questions.explanation: A is false: the products of burning are gases that escape into the air, so the mass only seems to disappear; if they were collected, the total mass would be unchanged. R is true: it is the Law of Conservation of Mass.

questions.stem: In a closed container, 10.0 g of calcium carbonate is heated until it decomposes completely into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide. If 5.6 g of calcium oxide is formed, what mass of carbon dioxide is formed? Name the law you used.
questions.answer: By the Law of Conservation of Mass, mass of reactants = mass of products. So mass of carbon dioxide = 10.0 g − 5.6 g = 4.4 g.
valuePoints: Mass of carbon dioxide = 10.0 − 5.6 = 4.4 g
Law of Conservation of Mass

rubric.label: Calculation
rubric.descriptor: 4.4 g, with working

rubric.label: Law
rubric.descriptor: Law of Conservation of Mass named

questions.stem: Write the symbols of sodium, potassium, iron and lead. Why do the symbols of these elements not match their English names?
questions.answer: Sodium Na, potassium K, iron Fe, lead Pb. These symbols come from the Latin names of the elements — natrium, kalium, ferrum and plumbum — following Berzelius's suggestion that symbols be derived from Latin names.
valuePoints: Na, K, Fe, Pb
Symbols are taken from Latin names (natrium, kalium, ferrum, plumbum)

rubric.label: Symbols
rubric.descriptor: All four correct; ½ mark for two or three correct

rubric.label: Reason
rubric.descriptor: Derived from the Latin names of the elements

questions.stem: Using the charges on the ions, write the chemical formulae of (i) aluminium sulfate and (ii) ammonium carbonate. Why are brackets used in these formulae?
questions.answer: (i) Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻: criss-crossing the charges gives Al₂(SO₄)₃. (ii) NH₄⁺ and CO₃²⁻: criss-crossing gives (NH₄)₂CO₃. Brackets are used when two or more polyatomic ions of the same type are present in the formula, so that the subscript applies to the whole ion.
valuePoints: Al₂(SO₄)₃
(NH₄)₂CO₃
Brackets enclose a polyatomic ion that occurs more than once

rubric.label: Formulae
rubric.descriptor: ½ mark each for Al₂(SO₄)₃ and (NH₄)₂CO₃

rubric.label: Use of brackets
rubric.descriptor: Two or more polyatomic ions of the same type; subscript applies to the whole ion

questions.stem: Magnesium oxide always contains magnesium and oxygen in the mass ratio 3 : 2. (i) What mass of oxygen combines with 12 g of magnesium? (ii) What mass of magnesium oxide is formed? (iii) If 12 g of magnesium is heated with 10 g of oxygen, which substance is left over, and how much?
questions.answer: (i) Oxygen = 12 g × 2/3 = 8 g. (ii) Magnesium oxide = 12 g + 8 g = 20 g (Law of Conservation of Mass). (iii) Only 8 g of oxygen can combine with 12 g of magnesium, because the ratio is fixed (Law of Constant Proportions). So 10 − 8 = 2 g of oxygen is left unreacted, and 20 g of magnesium oxide is still formed.
valuePoints: Oxygen needed = 8 g
Magnesium oxide formed = 20 g
2 g of oxygen left over, because the elements combine in a fixed ratio

rubric.label: Product mass
rubric.descriptor: 20 g of magnesium oxide

rubric.label: Excess reactant
rubric.descriptor: 2 g of oxygen left over (½), reason: fixed ratio by mass (½)

questions.stem: State any three postulates of Dalton's Atomic Theory. Show how one of them explains the Law of Conservation of Mass.
questions.answer: Any three of: all matter is made of very tiny particles called atoms, which take part in chemical reactions; atoms are indivisible and cannot be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction; atoms of a given element are identical in mass and chemical properties; atoms of different elements have different masses and chemical properties; atoms combine in the ratio of simple whole numbers to form compounds; the relative number and kinds of atoms are constant in a given compound. Explanation: since atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction but only rearrange, the same atoms, with the same masses, are present before and after the reaction, so the total mass stays the same.
valuePoints: Three correct postulates
Atoms are not created or destroyed; they only rearrange
So the total mass before and after the reaction is the same

rubric.label: Postulates
rubric.descriptor: ½ mark for each correct postulate, up to three

rubric.label: Explanation
rubric.descriptor: Atoms only rearrange (1); therefore total mass is unchanged (½)

questions.stem: Given the atomic masses H = 1 u, O = 16 u, S = 32 u and Al = 27 u, calculate (i) the molecular mass of sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄, and (ii) the formula unit mass of aluminium sulfate, Al₂(SO₄)₃. (iii) Why do we speak of a formula unit mass, and not a molecular mass, for aluminium sulfate?
questions.answer: (i) H₂SO₄ = (1 × 2) + (32 × 1) + (16 × 4) = 2 + 32 + 64 = 98 u. (ii) Al₂(SO₄)₃ = (27 × 2) + {(32 × 1) + (16 × 4)} × 3 = 54 + 96 × 3 = 54 + 288 = 342 u. (iii) Aluminium sulfate is an ionic compound; its ions form a three-dimensional crystal and do not form molecules, so we use the mass of the formula unit — the simplest whole-number ratio of its ions.
valuePoints: H₂SO₄ = 98 u
Al₂(SO₄)₃ = 342 u
Ionic compounds do not form molecules; a formula unit is the simplest ratio of ions

rubric.label: Molecular mass
rubric.descriptor: 98 u with working; ½ mark if unit missing

rubric.label: Formula unit mass
rubric.descriptor: 342 u with working, sulfate group multiplied by 3

rubric.label: Formula unit reason
rubric.descriptor: Ionic compound forms a crystal, not molecules; formula unit is simplest ratio of ions

questions.stem: Element A has the electronic configuration 2, 8, 3 and element B has 2, 6. (i) How many electrons does each tend to lose or gain, and what ions do they form? (ii) What type of bond is formed between them, and why? (iii) Write the formula of the compound by criss-crossing the charges. (iv) Identify A and B and calculate the formula unit mass of the compound (atomic masses: A = 27 u, B = 16 u). (v) Would this compound have a high or a low melting point? Give a reason.
questions.answer: (i) A has 3 valence electrons (fewer than four), so it loses 3 electrons to form the cation A³⁺. B has 6 valence electrons (more than four), so it gains 2 electrons to form the anion B²⁻. (ii) An ionic bond: electrons are transferred from A to B, and the oppositely charged ions are held together by electrostatic attraction. (iii) Charges 3+ and 2−; criss-crossing gives A₂B₃. (iv) A (atomic number 13) is aluminium and B (atomic number 8) is oxygen, so the compound is Al₂O₃. Formula unit mass = (27 × 2) + (16 × 3) = 54 + 48 = 102 u. (v) High, because ionic compounds have strong attractions between their ions.
valuePoints: A loses 3 electrons → A³⁺; B gains 2 electrons → B²⁻
Ionic bond by electron transfer and electrostatic attraction
Formula A₂B₃
Aluminium and oxygen; Al₂O₃ = 102 u
High melting point due to strong inter-ionic attraction

rubric.label: Ions formed
rubric.descriptor: ½ mark for A³⁺ (loses 3), ½ mark for B²⁻ (gains 2)

rubric.label: Type of bond
rubric.descriptor: Ionic, with electron transfer and attraction between opposite charges

rubric.label: Formula
rubric.descriptor: A₂B₃ by criss-crossing

rubric.label: Identity and mass
rubric.descriptor: Aluminium and oxygen (½); 102 u (½)

rubric.label: Melting point
rubric.descriptor: High (½) because of strong inter-ionic attraction (½)

questions.stem: (i) Explain how a chlorine molecule (Cl₂) is formed from two chlorine atoms (atomic number 17), and name the type of bond. (ii) Why are the two atoms in an oxygen molecule (O₂) joined by a double bond? (iii) Name the covalent compounds CS₂, N₂O₄ and SF₆. (iv) Using the valencies of carbon (4) and chlorine (1), write the formula of carbon tetrachloride.
questions.answer: (i) A chlorine atom (2, 8, 7) has seven valence electrons and needs one more to complete its octet. Two chlorine atoms each share one electron, forming one shared pair that holds them together: a single covalent bond, Cl–Cl. (ii) An oxygen atom (2, 6) has six valence electrons and needs two more. Two oxygen atoms each share two electrons, so two pairs of electrons are shared — a double bond, O=O. (iii) CS₂ carbon disulfide; N₂O₄ dinitrogen tetroxide; SF₆ sulfur hexafluoride. (iv) Write C and Cl with valencies 4 and 1, cross over the valencies as subscripts: CCl₄ (the subscript 1 is not written).
valuePoints: Each chlorine shares one electron; one shared pair; single covalent bond
Each oxygen needs two electrons; two shared pairs make a double bond
Carbon disulfide, dinitrogen tetroxide, sulfur hexafluoride
CCl₄ by crossing over valencies

rubric.label: Chlorine molecule
rubric.descriptor: Seven valence electrons, needs one (½); one electron shared by each, one shared pair (½); single covalent bond (½)

rubric.label: Oxygen double bond
rubric.descriptor: Needs two electrons (½); two shared pairs = double bond (½)

rubric.label: Names
rubric.descriptor: ½ mark for each correct name, including tetroxide (not tetraoxide)

rubric.label: Carbon tetrachloride
rubric.descriptor: CCl₄ with valencies crossed over

questions.passage: Two groups of students studied the reaction of zinc with dilute hydrochloric acid, which forms zinc chloride and hydrogen gas. Group 1 kept a conical flask of dilute acid and a few pieces of zinc on a digital balance, dropped the zinc into the open flask, and saw fizzing. Their reading fell from 120.50 g to 120.35 g. Group 2 put the zinc pieces inside a balloon, tied the balloon to the mouth of the flask, and then tipped the zinc into the acid. The balloon inflated, and the reading stayed at 121.10 g before and after the reaction. Later, their teacher mixed solutions of sodium sulfate and barium chloride in an open flask on the balance; a white precipitate formed and the reading did not change.

parts.prompt: Why did the reading of Group 1 decrease?

options.text: Some zinc was destroyed in the reaction
The hydrogen gas formed escaped from the open flask
Zinc chloride is lighter than zinc

parts.answer: (b) The hydrogen gas produced escaped into the air, so its mass was not recorded; no matter was destroyed.

parts.prompt: Which law is verified by the result of Group 2?
parts.answer: The Law of Conservation of Mass: the total mass before and after the reaction is the same.

parts.prompt: Why did the teacher not need a balloon for the reaction of sodium sulfate with barium chloride? What would be the mass of the products if the reactants had a total mass of 45.60 g?
parts.answer: No gas is formed in this reaction — the products are a barium sulfate precipitate and sodium chloride, which stay in the flask — so nothing escapes (1 mark). The products would have a total mass of 45.60 g, since mass is conserved (1 mark).

questions.assertion: Two astronauts doing a spacewalk outside a space station cannot hear each other speak directly.
questions.reason: Sound needs a material medium to propagate, and outer space is a near vacuum.
questions.answer: a
questions.explanation: Both are true, and R explains A: with almost no particles in space there is no medium to carry the sound, so the astronauts use communication devices fitted in their spacesuits.

questions.assertion: A sound wave of frequency 25 kHz can be heard by a person with normal hearing.
questions.reason: Animals such as dogs and bats can detect ultrasound.
questions.answer: d
questions.explanation: A is false: the human audible range is about 20 Hz to 20 kHz, and 25 kHz is ultrasonic. R is true: dogs, cats, bats and dolphins can detect ultrasound.

questions.stem: What are compressions and rarefactions in a sound wave? Why is a sound wave called a longitudinal wave?
questions.answer: A compression is a region of the medium where its density is higher than the average density; a rarefaction is a region where the density is lower than the average. A sound wave is longitudinal because the particles of the medium vibrate back and forth parallel to the direction in which the wave propagates.
valuePoints: Compression: region of higher than average density; rarefaction: region of lower than average density
Particles vibrate parallel to the direction of propagation

rubric.label: Compression and rarefaction
rubric.descriptor: ½ mark each, defined in terms of density compared with the average

rubric.label: Longitudinal
rubric.descriptor: Particle vibration parallel to the direction of wave propagation

questions.stem: At a point in air, 40 complete density oscillations occur in 0.2 s as a sound wave passes. Calculate the frequency and the time period of the wave.
questions.answer: Frequency ν = number of oscillations / time taken = 40 / 0.2 s = 200 Hz. Time period T = 1/ν = 1/200 s = 0.005 s (or 0.2 s / 40 = 0.005 s).

rubric.label: Frequency
rubric.descriptor: 200 Hz with unit

rubric.label: Time period
rubric.descriptor: 0.005 s with unit

questions.stem: During a thunderstorm, the thunder is heard 3 s after the lightning flash is seen. Taking the speed of sound in air as 340 m s⁻¹, how far away is the lightning? Why is the flash seen before the thunder is heard?
questions.answer: Distance = speed × time = 340 m s⁻¹ × 3 s = 1020 m (about 1 km). The flash is seen first because light travels far faster than sound (300000 km s⁻¹), so it reaches us almost instantly, while sound takes 3 s.
valuePoints: Distance = 340 × 3 = 1020 m
Light travels much faster than sound

rubric.label: Distance
rubric.descriptor: 1020 m with working

rubric.label: Reason
rubric.descriptor: Light is much faster than sound, reaches almost instantly

questions.stem: A tuning fork produces sound of frequency 500 Hz. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m s⁻¹ in air and 1500 m s⁻¹ in water, find (i) the wavelength of the sound in air, (ii) its time period, and (iii) its wavelength in water.
questions.answer: (i) λ = v/ν = 340 m s⁻¹ / 500 Hz = 0.68 m. (ii) T = 1/ν = 1/500 s = 0.002 s. (iii) λ = 1500 m s⁻¹ / 500 Hz = 3 m. The frequency is set by the source and stays 500 Hz; since the speed in water is greater, the wavelength is greater.
valuePoints: λ in air = 0.68 m
λ in water = 3 m

rubric.label: Wavelength in air
rubric.descriptor: v = νλ used; 0.68 m

rubric.label: Wavelength in water
rubric.descriptor: 3 m

questions.stem: What is meant by the loudness and the pitch of a sound? Which physical property of a sound wave is each mainly related to? When a metal plate is struck harder, which of the two changes, and why?
questions.answer: Pitch is how the frequency of a sound is perceived: a shrill sound such as a whistle has a high pitch and a higher frequency, while a deep sound such as thunder has a low pitch and a lower frequency. Loudness is how the amplitude of a sound wave is perceived: a larger amplitude sounds louder. Striking the plate harder transfers more energy to the medium, increasing the amplitude, so the sound becomes louder; its pitch does not change much.
valuePoints: Pitch: perception of frequency
Loudness: perception of amplitude
Striking harder increases amplitude and energy, so loudness increases

rubric.label: Pitch
rubric.descriptor: Perceived frequency; high frequency = high pitch

rubric.label: Loudness
rubric.descriptor: Perceived amplitude; larger amplitude = louder

rubric.label: Striking harder
rubric.descriptor: Loudness increases (½) because more energy gives larger amplitude (½)

questions.stem: Two sounds are heard separately only if they reach us at least 0.1 s apart. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m s⁻¹, find the minimum distance of a reflecting surface for an echo to be heard. Why is no echo heard in a small room?
questions.answer: In 0.1 s sound travels 340 m s⁻¹ × 0.1 s = 34 m. This is the distance to the reflecting surface and back, so the minimum distance of the surface is 34/2 = 17 m. In a small room the walls are much closer than 17 m, so the reflected sound arrives less than 0.1 s after the original sound and the brain cannot separate the two.
valuePoints: Distance travelled in 0.1 s = 34 m
Minimum distance = half of this = 17 m
In a small room reflections arrive within 0.1 s and are not heard separately

rubric.label: Minimum distance
rubric.descriptor: 17 m, halved because sound goes and returns

rubric.label: Small room
rubric.descriptor: Reflection returns in less than 0.1 s, cannot be distinguished

questions.stem: A ship uses sonar to study the sea below it. An ultrasonic pulse sent straight down returns after 3.0 s. Later, over a sunken wreck, the pulse returns after 2.4 s. The speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m s⁻¹. (i) What does sonar stand for, and on what principle does it work? (ii) Find the depth of the sea floor. (iii) Find the depth of the top of the wreck and how high the wreck rises above the sea floor. (iv) Name the animal ability on which sonar is modelled, and give one medical use of ultrasonic waves.
questions.answer: (i) Sonar stands for sound navigation and ranging. Ultrasonic waves are sent into water, and the reflected waves (echoes) are analysed to find the distance and direction of underwater objects. (ii) The pulse goes down and comes back, so the time to reach the floor = 3.0/2 = 1.5 s. Depth = 1500 m s⁻¹ × 1.5 s = 2250 m. (iii) Time to reach the wreck = 2.4/2 = 1.2 s; depth = 1500 × 1.2 = 1800 m. Height of wreck above the floor = 2250 − 1800 = 450 m. (iv) Echolocation, used by bats (and dolphins and whales) to locate obstacles and prey. Medical use: ultrasonography to image internal organs without surgery, or breaking kidney stones into small pieces.
valuePoints: Sonar: reflected ultrasonic waves used to find distance of underwater objects
Depth of floor = 1500 × 1.5 = 2250 m
Depth of wreck = 1800 m
Wreck rises 450 m above the floor
Echolocation; ultrasonography or breaking kidney stones

rubric.label: Sonar principle
rubric.descriptor: Full form (½); reflection of ultrasonic waves to locate objects (½)

rubric.label: Sea floor depth
rubric.descriptor: Halves the time (½); 2250 m (1)

rubric.label: Wreck
rubric.descriptor: 1800 m (1); 450 m above the floor (½)

rubric.label: Echolocation and medical use
rubric.descriptor: ½ mark each

questions.stem: Two friends stand 1020 m apart beside a long steel railing. One knocks the railing with a metal object while the other keeps an ear against it. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m s⁻¹ in air and 5000 m s⁻¹ in steel: (i) find the time taken by the sound to reach the listener through air and through steel; (ii) find the time difference and state whether the listener hears two separate sounds (two sounds must be at least 0.1 s apart to be heard separately); (iii) how many times faster is sound in steel than in air here? (iv) Arrange solids, liquids and gases in order of the speed of sound in them.
questions.answer: (i) Through air: t = 1020 m / 340 m s⁻¹ = 3 s. Through steel: t = 1020 m / 5000 m s⁻¹ = 0.204 s. (ii) Difference = 3 − 0.204 = 2.796 s ≈ 2.8 s. This is much more than 0.1 s, so the listener hears two separate sounds — first through the steel, then through the air. (iii) 5000/340 ≈ 14.7, so sound is about 15 times faster in steel. (iv) Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases.
valuePoints: Time in air = 3 s
Time in steel = 0.204 s
Difference ≈ 2.8 s, more than 0.1 s, so two sounds heard
Steel about 14.7 times faster
Solids > liquids > gases

rubric.descriptor: 3 s using t = d/v

rubric.label: Difference and conclusion
rubric.descriptor: 2.796 s (½); two separate sounds because it exceeds 0.1 s (½)

rubric.label: Ratio
rubric.descriptor: About 14.7 (accept 15)

rubric.label: Order of media
rubric.descriptor: Solids fastest, then liquids, gases slowest

questions.passage: In a classroom demonstration, Farhan whistled a steady note into a mobile phone running a sound app that shows frequency. The app showed that the whistle was almost a single frequency of 1720 Hz. The teacher explained that everyday sounds usually contain a mixture of many frequencies, but a whistle or a struck tuning fork gives nearly a single frequency. The speed of sound in the classroom air was taken as 344 m s⁻¹. Farhan then whistled a higher note, and the app showed a frequency of 3440 Hz.

parts.prompt: The first whistle, of frequency 1720 Hz, is

options.text: too fast to have a wavelength

parts.answer: (b) The human audible range is about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, and 1720 Hz lies within it.

parts.prompt: Calculate the wavelength of the first whistle in air.
For the second note of 3440 Hz, what are the speed and the wavelength of the sound in the same air? Explain.
parts.answer: The speed stays 344 m s⁻¹, because in air the speed of sound depends on the medium and not on the frequency (1 mark). Since v = νλ, doubling the frequency halves the wavelength: λ = 344/3440 = 0.1 m (1 mark).

questions.assertion: Sugarcane plants grown from stem cuttings of one parent plant are genetically identical to that parent.
questions.reason: The cells of a stem cutting are formed by meiosis.
questions.answer: c
questions.explanation: A is true: vegetative propagation involves only one parent, so the offspring are genetically identical clones. R is false: the growth of a new plant from a cutting involves mitosis, which keeps the chromosomes identical; meiosis forms gametes.

questions.assertion: Human sperm and eggs each contain 23 chromosomes.
questions.reason: Human sperm are actively motile, whereas the egg is non-motile.
questions.answer: b
questions.explanation: Both are true, but R does not explain A. Gametes have 23 chromosomes because they are formed by meiosis, which halves the chromosome number of 46; motility is a separate difference between the two gametes.

questions.stem: Why must gametes be formed by meiosis and not by mitosis?
questions.answer: In sexual reproduction two gametes fuse to form a zygote. If gametes were formed by mitosis, each would have the full set of chromosomes (46 in humans), and the chromosome number would double in every generation. Meiosis halves the chromosome number (46 to 23), so when a sperm and an egg fuse, the zygote has 46 chromosomes, the same as the parents.
valuePoints: Mitosis would give gametes a full set, doubling chromosome number every generation
Meiosis halves it, so the zygote has the parents' number (23 + 23 = 46)

rubric.label: Problem with mitosis
rubric.descriptor: Chromosome number would double in each generation

rubric.label: Role of meiosis
rubric.descriptor: Halves the number so the zygote restores 46

questions.stem: Name the three parts of the pistil of a flower. State the function of the stigma and of the ovary.
questions.answer: The pistil has the stigma, the style and the ovary. The stigma, at the tip and often sticky, receives the pollen grains. The ovary contains the ovules, each with an egg cell; after fertilisation the ovules become seeds and the ovary develops into the fruit.
valuePoints: Stigma, style, ovary
Stigma receives pollen; ovary holds the ovules with egg cells and becomes the fruit

rubric.descriptor: All three; ½ mark for two

questions.stem: Give two differences between the human sperm and the egg.
questions.answer: Any two: the sperm is very small while the egg is large; sperm are produced in millions while usually one egg is released each month; the sperm has no stored nutrients while the egg has stored nutrients; the sperm is actively motile (it has a tail) while the egg is non-motile.

questions.stem: Describe how (i) hydra reproduces by budding and (ii) bread mould reproduces by spores. (iii) Why are the offspring in both cases genetically identical to the parent?
questions.answer: (i) In hydra, repeated cell division at a particular site on the parent's body produces a small outgrowth called a bud; it enlarges and separates to live independently. (ii) Bread mould forms huge numbers of tiny, lightweight spores inside sac-like structures at the tips of its hyphae; the spores float in air and, on reaching a moist surface with nutrients, germinate into new moulds. (iii) Both involve only one parent, and the cells are produced by mitosis, which gives daughter cells with the same chromosomes as the parent cell, so the offspring are clones.

Spores formed in sacs, carried by air, germinate on moist food
One parent and mitosis, so identical offspring

questions.stem: Compare wind-pollinated and insect-pollinated flowers, giving the features of each and one example of each.
questions.answer: Wind-pollinated flowers (for example wheat, maize, rice): pollen grains are light and small and produced in very large numbers; the stigma is long and feathery to trap pollen from the air. Insect-pollinated flowers (for example sunflower, hibiscus, marigold): flowers are often brightly coloured, produce nectar and give off fragrance to attract insects; pollen grains are large, sticky or spiny so they stick to the insect's body, and the stigma is sticky to receive them.

Insect: bright colour, nectar, fragrance; sticky or spiny pollen; sticky stigma

questions.stem: In the human menstrual cycle, explain what happens to the inner lining of the uterus (i) when the released egg is not fertilised and (ii) when it is fertilised. (iii) Why does menstruation stop during pregnancy?
questions.answer: (i) Before and after ovulation the lining of the uterus becomes thick and rich in blood vessels. If the egg is not fertilised, it degenerates in about a day, the lining is not needed and it sheds, leaving the body with some blood as menstruation, which usually lasts 3 to 7 days. (ii) If the egg is fertilised, the zygote divides by mitosis as it travels to the uterus and implants in the thickened lining, which nourishes it; implantation marks the beginning of pregnancy. (iii) During pregnancy the lining is needed to protect and nourish the developing embryo and foetus, so it is not shed, and menstruation stops.
valuePoints: Unfertilised egg: thickened lining sheds as menstruation
Fertilised: zygote implants in the thickened lining
Lining is kept to nourish the embryo, so no menstruation

rubric.descriptor: Lining sheds with blood (menstruation)

rubric.label: Egg fertilised
rubric.descriptor: Zygote implants in the thickened lining; pregnancy begins

rubric.label: Why menstruation stops
rubric.descriptor: Lining is retained to nourish the developing baby

questions.stem: Describe the events in a flowering plant from pollination to the formation of a fruit with seeds. Distinguish between self-pollination and cross-pollination in your answer.
questions.answer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma. If pollen reaches the stigma of the same flower or of another flower on the same plant, it is self-pollination; if it reaches the stigma of a flower on another plant of the same type, it is cross-pollination. Pollinators such as wind, water, insects and birds carry the pollen. On a compatible stigma the pollen grain produces a pollen tube, which grows down through the style into the ovary and reaches the ovule. The male gamete moves through the tube and fuses with the egg cell in the ovule — this is fertilisation. The fertilised egg is the zygote, which develops into an embryo. Meanwhile the ovule develops into the seed and the ovary enlarges into the fruit. Seeds are dispersed by wind, water or animals and germinate into new plants when conditions are favourable.
valuePoints: Pollination: anther to stigma; self vs cross distinguished
Pollen tube grows through the style to the ovule
Male gamete fuses with egg: fertilisation, zygote
Zygote to embryo; ovule to seed
Ovary to fruit

rubric.descriptor: Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma, with an agent

rubric.label: Self and cross
rubric.descriptor: ½ mark each for correct distinction

rubric.label: Pollen tube
rubric.descriptor: Grows through style into ovary to reach ovule

rubric.label: Fertilisation
rubric.descriptor: Male gamete fuses with egg to form zygote, which becomes the embryo

rubric.label: Seed and fruit
rubric.descriptor: Ovule becomes seed (½); ovary becomes fruit (½)

questions.stem: (i) Distinguish between mitosis and meiosis. (ii) In a bead activity, a student takes three pairs of beads, each pair standing for two contrasting characters on one pair of chromosomes, and picks one bead from each pair to make a gamete. How many different combinations are possible? Show how you get the number. (iii) Explain how meiosis in humans, who have 23 pairs of chromosomes, leads to variation, and why variation matters for a species.
questions.answer: (i) Mitosis produces two daughter cells with the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell, identical to it; it is used in growth and in asexual reproduction. Meiosis halves the chromosome number (diploid to haploid), separating the chromosomes of each pair, and forms gametes. (ii) Each of the three pairs gives 2 choices, so the number of combinations = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. (iii) In meiosis the chromosomes of each of the 23 pairs separate at random, so each gamete receives one chromosome of every pair in a new combination, and the possible combinations are enormous. Fertilisation then combines two such gametes, so children differ from their parents and from their siblings. Variation helps some individuals adapt better when the environment changes, which aids the survival of the species and, over time, contributes to evolution.
valuePoints: Mitosis: identical cells with same chromosome number; meiosis: halves number to form gametes
2 × 2 × 2 = 8 combinations
Random separation of 23 pairs gives a huge number of gamete combinations
Offspring differ from parents and siblings
Variation helps adaptation and survival of the species

rubric.label: Combinations
rubric.descriptor: 8, shown as 2 × 2 × 2

rubric.label: Source of variation
rubric.descriptor: Random separation of pairs (1); unique offspring (½)

rubric.label: Importance of variation
rubric.descriptor: Adaptation to changing environment and survival of species

questions.passage: Students of a school eco-club studied pea plants in their garden. On one plant they chose two young, unopened flower buds and two freshly opened flowers. They carefully removed the stamens from one bud and from one open flower. Then they tied loose muslin cloth bags over all four so that no insect or wind-blown pollen could reach them, and left a fifth open flower uncovered. After two weeks they found that pods had formed from the uncovered flower, from the bagged bud with stamens, from both bagged open flowers, but not from the bagged bud whose stamens had been removed.

parts.prompt: The experiment mainly shows that fruit formation needs

options.text: the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma

parts.answer: (b) Only the bud that could receive no pollen at all failed to form a pod, so pollination is necessary for fruit formation.

parts.prompt: The bagged bud that still had its stamens formed a pod. Which type of pollination took place in it?
parts.answer: Self-pollination: pollen from its own anthers reached its own stigma inside the bag.

parts.prompt: Why did the open flower with its stamens removed still form a pod, while the bud with its stamens removed did not?
parts.answer: The open flower had already bloomed, so pollen had probably reached its stigma before the stamens were removed and the bag was tied (1 mark). The bud's stamens were removed before its pollen was released, and the bag kept out other pollen, so no pollination and no fertilisation occurred (1 mark).

questions.assertion: Bacteria are placed in kingdom Monera, while Amoeba is placed in kingdom Protista.
questions.reason: Bacteria do not have a membrane-bound nucleus, whereas Amoeba has a true, membrane-bound nucleus.

questions.reason: Pteridophytes have vascular tissues, xylem and phloem, to transport water and food.
questions.answer: d

questions.stem: Arrange the following levels of classification from the broadest to the most specific: genus, kingdom, order, species, class, family, phylum. At which level do the members share the most features?

questions.answer: Mangifera is the genus and indica is the species. Rules (any two): the genus name comes first and begins with a capital letter; the species name follows in small letters; the name is printed in italics or underlined when handwritten.

questions.stem: State the four criteria used in the five kingdom classification. Apply them to a mushroom to show why it belongs to kingdom Fungi.
questions.answer: Criteria: cell type (prokaryote or eukaryote); cell structure (presence or absence of a cell wall); level of organisation (unicellular or multicellular); mode of nutrition (autotrophic or heterotrophic). A mushroom is eukaryotic, has a cell wall (made of chitin), is multicellular, and is heterotrophic — it absorbs nutrients from dead and decaying matter and does not make its own food. So it belongs to Fungi, not Plantae.

questions.stem: Give one distinguishing feature each of bryophytes, pteridophytes and gymnosperms, and name one example of each group.
questions.answer: Bryophytes (moss, Marchantia): slightly differentiated body with rhizoids, no true roots, stems or leaves and no vascular tissue; need water for reproduction. Pteridophytes (fern): true roots, stems and leaves with xylem and phloem, but no seeds, and still need water for reproduction. Gymnosperms (pine, cycad): produce seeds that are not enclosed in fruits (exposed on cones), do not need water for fertilisation, and have needle-like or scale-like leaves.

questions.stem: Compare Porifera, Cnidaria and Platyhelminthes with respect to their level of body organisation and how they obtain food.
questions.answer: Porifera (sponges): multicellular but with no tissues or organs (cellular level); numerous pores let water flow through the body, bringing food particles and oxygen to the cells. Cnidaria (hydra, jellyfish): tissue level of organisation; they capture prey with tentacles, and a single opening serves for both taking in food and removing waste. Platyhelminthes (flatworms): organ level of organisation with bilateral symmetry; many are parasites that attach to the host with hooks and suckers to obtain nutrients, and they too have a single opening.

questions.stem: (i) What is a notochord, and how is it used to divide the animal kingdom? (ii) Give the distinguishing features of Nematoda, Annelida, Arthropoda and Echinodermata, with one example of each.
questions.answer: (i) A notochord is a flexible rod-shaped structure. Animals without a notochord are non-chordates (invertebrates); animals that have one at least at some stage are chordates, which include protochordates (such as Amphioxus) and vertebrates, in which the notochord is a precursor of the vertebral column. (ii) Nematoda (roundworms): elongated cylindrical body with two openings, mouth and anus. Annelida (earthworm): cylindrical body divided into segments, with a body cavity, muscles for locomotion and a nerve cord. Arthropoda (insects, crabs, spiders): segmented body with jointed appendages and a hard external skeleton that protects and reduces water loss. Echinodermata (starfish, sea urchin): spiny skin and a hard internal skeleton of calcium carbonate, but no notochord; marine.

questions.stem: Kingdom Plantae is divided into five groups, from Thallophyta to Angiosperms. Explain how the groups show a gradual reduction in dependence on water, with reference to body organisation, transport tissue, seeds and fruits.
questions.answer: Thallophyta (algae such as Spirogyra) have a simple thallus body that exchanges gases, nutrients and water directly with the surroundings; they live in water or moist places. Bryophyta (mosses, Marchantia) began to colonise land, with rhizoids and simple stem-like and leaf-like parts, but no vascular tissue; they need water for reproduction, so they are the amphibians of the plant kingdom. Pteridophyta (ferns) have true roots, stems and leaves and vascular tissue (xylem and phloem) to carry water and food through the plant, but they produce no seeds and still need water for reproduction. Gymnosperms (pines, cycads) produce seeds that protect the embryo and store food, do not need water for fertilisation, and have needle-like leaves that reduce water loss; their seeds are not enclosed in fruits. Angiosperms (flowering plants) have well-developed roots, stems and leaves, reproduce through flowers that attract pollinators, and enclose their seeds in fruits that help disperse them — so they occupy the widest range of environments.

Angiosperms: flowers, seeds in fruits

questions.answer: Tree roots hold the soil together; when the forest is cleared, nothing holds the soil, so rain and run-off wash it away. Soil erosion can be reduced by planting trees (or by sustainable farming practices).

questions.stem: Describe the oxygen cycle: name the processes that use up atmospheric oxygen and the process that restores it, and explain why the balance between them matters.
questions.answer: Oxygen is used up by the respiration of plants and animals, which releases carbon dioxide, and by the combustion of fuels, which also releases carbon dioxide. It is restored mainly by photosynthesis, in which plants use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make glucose and release oxygen. The balance between consumption and production keeps the amount of oxygen in the atmosphere (about 21%) roughly steady, sustaining life across all the spheres of the Earth.

questions.stem: Explain how the atmosphere keeps the Earth warm enough for life. Why is an excess of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere a problem, even though plants need it?
questions.answer: The Earth's surface absorbs sunlight and re-radiates heat in the infrared region. Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour absorb part of this outgoing heat and prevent it from escaping into space; without this, the Earth would be too cold for life. Excess carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels and deforestation enhances this greenhouse effect, causing global warming, which melts glaciers and sea ice, raises sea levels and brings more extreme weather.

questions.stem: What is eutrophication? Explain how the overuse of fertilisers on farms can lead to the death of fish in a nearby lake.
questions.answer: Eutrophication is the process in which excess nutrients in a water body cause a widespread growth of algae (an algal bloom) that depletes oxygen. When too much fertiliser is used, excess nitrogen as nitrates is washed from the fields into rivers and lakes. The nitrates cause algae to grow rapidly; the algal bloom depletes the oxygen dissolved in the water, and the fish die for lack of oxygen, threatening water bodies and fisheries.

questions.stem: Describe the carbon cycle, distinguishing its fast and slow parts and the role of the oceans. How have human activities disturbed it, and what are the consequences?
questions.answer: Carbon circulates between the atmosphere (CO₂), the biosphere (plants and animals), the geosphere (carbonate rocks and fossil fuels) and the hydrosphere (dissolved CO₂ and marine shells). Fast cycle (days to years): plants take in atmospheric CO₂ and make glucose by photosynthesis; plants and animals release CO₂ by respiration; when organisms die, decomposition returns CO₂ to the air. Slow cycle (millions of years): buried dead plants and animals turn into fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas. Oceans exchange CO₂ with the atmosphere; dissolved CO₂ forms carbonate and bicarbonate ions used by phytoplankton in photosynthesis and by some organisms to make shells, and dead organisms store carbon on the ocean floor. Human activities — burning fossil fuels, which releases in a short time carbon stored over millions of years, and deforestation, which reduces photosynthesis — have raised atmospheric CO₂ from about 315 ppm in 1960 to about 420 ppm. This intensifies the greenhouse effect, causing global warming, melting glaciers and sea ice, rising sea levels and extreme weather, and makes sea water more acidic, threatening plankton and coral reefs.
valuePoints: Reservoirs: atmosphere, biosphere, geosphere, hydrosphere
Fast cycle: photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition
Slow cycle: fossil fuel formation over millions of years
Oceans absorb CO₂; shells and phytoplankton
Human impact: fossil fuels and deforestation raise CO₂; warming and ocean acidity

questions.stem: (i) The insolation at a place on a clear day is 1 kW m⁻². How much solar energy falls on a solar panel of area 2 m² in 30 minutes? (ii) Why do snow-covered regions stay colder than regions of black soil receiving the same sunlight? (iii) In the troposphere the temperature falls by about 6.5 °C for every kilometre of height. If the ground temperature is 30 °C, estimate the temperature at a height of 4 km. (iv) Why does the temperature rise with height in the stratosphere?
questions.answer: (i) E = intensity × area × time = 1000 J s⁻¹ m⁻² × 2 m² × (30 × 60) s = 1000 × 2 × 1800 J = 3 600 000 J = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. (ii) Albedo is the fraction of solar radiation reflected by a surface. Snow has a high albedo (about 0.80–0.90), so it reflects most of the sunlight and absorbs little; black soil has a low albedo, absorbs more radiation and warms up. (iii) Fall in temperature = 6.5 °C/km × 4 km = 26 °C, so the temperature ≈ 30 − 26 = 4 °C. (iv) The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere; ozone absorbs UV rays from the Sun and heats that layer, so its temperature increases with height.
valuePoints: Snow has high albedo, reflects more; black soil absorbs more
Temperature at 4 km ≈ 4 °C
Ozone absorbs UV and heats the stratosphere

questions.passage: A farmer in Madhya Pradesh grows soybean, a legume, in the rainy season and wheat in winter. When she pulled out a soybean plant, her daughter noticed small round swellings, called root nodules, on its roots. The local agriculture officer explained that bacteria living in these nodules convert nitrogen gas from the air into ammonia, so the next crop needs less fertiliser. He also warned that some farmers in the village spread far more nitrate fertiliser than their crops can use, and that the extra nitrates are washed into the village pond with the rain. He added that some soil bacteria convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas, which returns to the air.

parts.prompt: Which bacterium lives in the root nodules of legumes and fixes atmospheric nitrogen?
parts.answer: (c) Rhizobium in the root nodules of legumes converts atmospheric N₂ into ammonia (nitrogen fixation).

parts.prompt: Name the process by which soil bacteria convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas.
parts.answer: Denitrification (carried out by bacteria such as Pseudomonas).

parts.prompt: What is likely to happen to the fish in the village pond if excess nitrates keep reaching it? Explain.
parts.answer: The nitrates cause a rapid, widespread growth of algae — an algal bloom (eutrophication) (1 mark). The bloom depletes the oxygen in the water, so the fish may die (1 mark).
